edges.description: Both are found in the heterozygous mouse; which transcriptional targets limit brain growth is not known.
The founding report proposes reduced neuronal proliferation or survival as an explanation for microcephaly; this has not been tested in the heterozygous mouse.

Purkinje cells are where BCL11A is most highly expressed in the developing cerebellum, and the vermis is the structure most often small in patients; that Purkinje cell dysfunction is the cause has not been shown.

nodes.description: Heterozygous frameshift, stop-gain and splice variants, deletions of the gene, and a small number of missense variants. Missense variants clustered in the N-terminal region disrupt nuclear localization, dimerization and transcriptional regulatory activity of BCL11A; N-terminal C2HC zinc-finger variants increase proteasomal degradation, and a C-terminal zinc-finger variant abolishes DNA binding. All of these are loss-of-function alleles, and ClinGen and the founding report treat haploinsufficiency as the mechanism. BCL11A is a dedicated subunit of the BAF (SWI/SNF) chromatin-remodeling complex, which places the disorder among the BAFopathies.

Persistence of HbF is the main erythroid consequence; hematologic and immunologic function are otherwise normal.

nodes.description: In the developing mouse neocortex Bcl11a directly represses Sema3c in migrating upper-layer neurons, which is required for their multipolar-to-bipolar switch and radial migration; it directly represses Tbr1 in layer 5 to specify subcerebral projection neurons; and through Bcl6 it supports survival of upper-layer projection neurons during postnatal corticogenesis. In cortical progenitors, conditional loss reduces proliferation and causes precocious differentiation, probably through derepression of Nr2f1, and in layer IV it is needed for sensory area identity and thalamocortical input fields. These findings come from homozygous or conditional knockouts, not from the heterozygous state seen in patients.
